https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.title: Simple screening reveals unmanaged CV risk in psoriasis patients
https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.author: Regina Schaffer
https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Nearly half of patients with psoriasis screened for cardiovascular disease risk factors at the recommendation of their dermatologist had elevated blood pressure, cholesterol or HbA1c, suggesting a need for improved care coordination.

The findings, presented in a poster during the Society for Investigative Dermatology Annual Meeting, also showed people with psoriasis want to engage in proactive measures that will reduce their disease burden, according to Joel M. Gelfand, MD, MSCE, FAAD, Healio Dermatology’s Chief Medical Editor and one of the study’s co-authors.

“About 80% of patients completed blood work for cholesterol and diabetes and recorded home blood pressure readings, demonstrating the high motivation of psoriasis patients to undergo CV risk factor screening when recommended by their dermatologist,” Gelfand told Healio. “Nearly 50% of patients had modifiable CV risk factors that require medical management per guidelines, demonstrating a large evidence-to-practice gap when it comes to CV risk factor management in psoriasis patients.”

People with psoriasis are at higher risk for cardiovascular disease, yet CV risk factors are often inadequately measured in clinical practice, according to Guy S. Eakin, PhD, chief scientific and medical officer for the National Psoriasis Foundation and study co-author.

“Psoriasis is not just a skin disease. It is our first warning that there is a systemic inflammatory condition happening inside the body,” Eakin told Healio. “There is growing recognition that we can add years back to people’s lives by thinking about secondary prevention. That is what makes this project transformational.”

For the study, the researchers screened 585 patients with psoriasis but without known cardiovascular disease at baseline from 22 dermatology practices across the U.S. Patients ranged in age from 40 to 75 years (median age; 53 years), 57.3% were women and 82.2% were white. The mean body surface area involvement for patients was 4.5%. Participating clinics represented a diversity of practice areas, including 10 academic centers, 11 private practices and one private telehealth practice.

All patients received dermatologist-delivered education about psoriasis-associated CV risk. For patients with complete screening data, researchers calculated their 10-year CV risk using the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association 2018 atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk estimator. Patients with an estimated 10-year CV risk that was 5% or higher were referred to a psoriasis care coordination model.

Among the 454 patients with a calculated CVD risk, 47% required intervention. More than 30% of patients had an ASCVD 10-year risk of 5% or higher, and more than 10% had a 10-year risk of less than 5% but uncontrolled risk factors. The dermatologist-led screenings also revealed that nearly 20% of patients had newly identified CV risk markers, including uncontrolled hypertension, hyperlipidemia and type 2 diabetes.

“What the dermatology community should walk away with [from this study] is that half of your patients are walking through the door with psoriasis, but they are also coming with unmanaged, likely undiagnosed, elevated CVD risk,” Eakin told Healio. “Dermatologists have an opportunity to engage in lifesaving care, and their psoriasis patients are very motivated to undergo this risk factor screening.”

Referring patients with psoriasis and elevated CV risk to a centralized care coordination center not only helps to close the gap between a diagnosis and education but also leads to action that directly improves the health of patients, according to Tiffany Bass, a study care coordinator with the NPF.

“A care coordinator is going to provide targeted education and help the patient understand the link between psoriasis and conditions like high cholesterol, hypertension and diabetes, which makes that risk more tangible and actionable,” Bass told Healio.

“A lot of times patients will be told about their risk and it gets pushed to the back burner,” Bass said. “When you have a care coordinator who is checking in with you, asking, ‘Have you met with your primary care doctor? Have you discussed these things? Have you taken your blood pressure again?’ That follow-up turns abstract advice into practical behavior changes.”

Tiffany Bass is a study care coordinator with the NPF. Bass can be reached at tbass@psoriasis.org.

Guy S. Eakin, PhD, is chief scientific and medical officer for the NPF. Eakin can be reached at geakin@psoriasis.org.

Joel M. Gelfand, MD, MSCE, FAAD, is Chief Medical Editor of Healio Dermatology. Gelfand can be reached at dermatology@healio.com.

Kernizan F, et al. Poster #493. Presented at: Society for Investigative Dermatology Annual Meeting; May 13-16, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: The NPF funded this study. Gelfand is Chief Medical Editor of Healio Dermatology. Bass and Eakin report no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: New drug reduces inflammatory biomarkers in high-risk patients
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

A novel NLRP3 inhibitor reduced high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and other inflammatory biomarkers in patients at high inflammatory risk, according to the results of a trial presented at the European Atherosclerosis Society Congress.

The NLRP3 inhibitor, ruvonoflast (NodThera), “is designed to directly inhibit activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in multiple clinically relevant cell types (eg, macrophages, vascular cells),” Jyothis P. George, MD, PhD, chief medical officer of NodThera and an author of the study, told Healio. “By targeting NLRP3, ruvonoflast aims to reduce the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (eg, interleukin [IL]-1-beta and IL-18, with downstream effects on IL-6), which are implicated in cardiovascular and metabolic disease biology.”

For the phase 1b study, simultaneously published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, George and colleagues randomly assigned 63 patients with hsCRP at least 2.5 mg/L, BMI between 30 kg/m2 and 40 kg/m2 and dyslipidemia, hypertension or diabetes (mean age, 52.6 years; 71.4% women; median baseline hsCRP, 5.7 mg/L) to ruvonoflast 225 mg twice daily or placebo.

“The NLRP3 inflammasome is an intracellular multiprotein complex that helps regulate the inflammatory responses as a key component of the innate immune system,” George told Healio. “In cardiometabolic diseases, chronic activation of the NLRP3 pathway triggered by cardiometabolic stimuli like cholesterol crystals can drive persistent low-grade inflammation, which contributes to atherosclerosis progression, plaque instability, insulin resistance and broader cardiovascular risk. Inhibiting NLRP3 is compelling ... because it targets an upstream regulator of inflammation, with the potential to simultaneously modulate multiple downstream mediators (including IL-1, IL-6 and IL-18) that contribute to both cardiovascular and metabolic disease processes.”

The primary outcome of change in hsCRP at 28 days favored the ruvonoflast group (82.2% vs. 37.2%; P < .001), and the curves started to separate at day 3, according to the researchers.

Ruvonoflast was also associated with greater reductions in IL-6 and fibrinogen at 28 days compared with placebo (P < .001 for both), the researchers found.

The rate of treatment-emergent adverse events was similar in both groups, though four patients in the ruvonoflast group discontinued the study medication due to treatment-emergent adverse events compared with none in the placebo group, according to the researchers.

In addition, “76% of ruvonoflast-treated patients achieved hsCRP < 2 mg/L, an on-treatment threshold associated with 25% major adverse CV event reduction in the CANTOS trial of canakinumab (Ilaris, Novartis), an IL-1-beta blocker, underscoring the potential for meaningful event reduction if translated to outcomes,” George told Healio. “The safety and efficacy package from this trial, together with prior data in Parkinson’s disease, has enabled the phase 2 RESOLVE-1 and RESOLVE-2 trials, the largest and longest NLRP3 studies to date, and underpins ongoing phase 3 development. The RESOLVE-1 trial is assessing ruvonoflast as monotherapy while RESOLVE-2 is evaluating ruvonoflast in combination with GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy. Both studies, expected to read out in 2026, will also provide broader safety experience, including evaluation across larger populations and longer treatment durations up to 32 weeks while incorporating additional biomarker, metabolic and imaging endpoints.”

Jyothis P. George, MD, PhD, can be reached at jyothis.george@nodthera.com; LinkedIn www.linkedin.com/company/nodthera; X @NodThera.

Ray KK, et al. Late breaker clinical abstracts. Presented at: European Atherosclerosis Society Congress; May 24-27, 2026; Athens, Greece.

Disclosures: George reports being an employee of NodThera. Please see the study for all other authors’ relevant financial disclosures. The study was funded by NodThera.

https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.title: GLP-1/GIP dual agonist lowers HbA1c, weight in type 1 diabetes
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.author: Michael Monostra
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

NEW ORLEANS — A once-daily GLP-1/GIP dual agonist reduced HbA1c and body weight at 16 weeks among adults with type 1 diabetes, according to findings from a phase 2 trial presented at the American Diabetes Association Scientific Sessions.

Acmopatide (Roche), formerly known as CT-868, delivered a wide range of benefits among people with type 1 diabetes. Beyond improvements in HbA1c and body weight, participants receiving 4.1 mg or 6.6 mg of the study drug also had improvements in blood pressure and heart rate than those receiving placebo.

Despite these benefits, Jeremy Pettus, MD, associate professor of medicine at University of California, San Diego, said Roche has decided not to move forward with a phase 3 trial for acmopatide.

“I think I speak for my other colleagues and speakers that we’re very disappointed with this announcement,” Pettus said during a presentation. “As somebody that’s been fighting this cause for a long time, living with type 1 diabetes, we have such an urgent need for metabolic therapies for type 1 diabetes. This is quite devastating, to be honest.”

The phase 2 trial enrolled 111 adults aged 18 to 65 years with type 1 diabetes, an HbA1c of 7% to 10% at baseline, and a BMI of 27 kg/m2 or higher. Participants were randomly assigned to acmopatide 1.8 mg, 4.1 mg or 6.6 mg, or placebo for 16 weeks. The primary outcome was change in HbA1c from baseline to 16 weeks.

At 16 weeks, the acmopatide 4.1 mg group had a 0.59 percentage point decrease in HbA1c compared with a 0.25 percentage point decline with placebo (P < .05). There was no difference in change in HbA1c between the other two acmopatide groups and placebo.

At 16 weeks, 55.6% of the acmopatide 4.1 mg group and 43.5% of the acmopatide 6.6 mg group reached an HbA1c of less than 7% compared with 33.3% of the placebo group.

Klara Klein, MD, PhD, assistant professor of medicine at University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, said the study’s short duration means a higher percentage of adults receiving acmopatide may have been able to reach an HbA1c of less than 7% if they received the drug for a longer period.

“While I think you can appreciate that placebo looked like it was reaching plateau, no arms in the acmopatide group looked like they had reached plateau,” Klein said during a presentation.

Klein said continuous glucose monitoring metrics were slightly better among the acmopatide groups compared with placebo, and clinically significant hypoglycemia did not increase with the study medication.

“There were numerical increases in time below 54 mg/dL in the acmopatide groups,” Klein said. “But all groups on average remained under the [American Diabetes Association recommended] target of less than 1% time below 54 mg/dL. These are really low percentages.”

At 16 weeks, weight loss with acmopatide was 6.67% with the 6.6 mg dose, 6.43% with the 4.1 mg dose and 3.26% with the 1.8 mg dose compared with a 0.29% weight gain with placebo (P < .01 for all).

The percentage of adults reaching a 5% or greater weight loss with acmopatide was 63% in both the acmopatide 4.1 mg and 6.6 mg groups, and 34.6% with acmopatide 1.8 mg compared with 7.4% with placebo.

Adults receiving acmopatide 6.6 mg had a 14.92 U reduction in total insulin use from baseline to 16 weeks.

Systolic blood pressure decreased by 8.4 mm Hg in the acmopatide 6.6 mg group and 5 mm Hg with the 4.1 mg dose compared with 3.3 mm Hg with placebo. Change in diastolic BP was similar between all four groups. From baseline to 16 weeks, heart rate increased by 6.5 beats per minute (bpm) with acmopatide 6.6 mg and 6.9 bpm with the 4.1 mg dose compared with a 2.1 bpm increase with placebo.

The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal in nature and included nausea, constipation, vomiting, decreased appetite and diarrhea. Gastrointestinal adverse events were mostly mild to moderate in severity.

There were no reports of level three hypoglycemia or diabetic ketoacidosis during the trial.

Pettus noted that patient-reported treatment satisfaction was also higher with acmopatide than placebo.

“The good news here is that we’ve learned a lot from previous trials that these drugs might not cause hypoglycemia, but they certainly do in the study of insulin administration,” Pettus said. “I think we’ve gotten better at how to start these drugs and reduce insulin prophylactically to keep people in a safe range.”

Pettus said it was disappointing that acmopatide would not move forward with phase 3 trials, but he feels that there is hope that an incretin-based medication could be FDA approved for type 1 diabetes in the future. Eli Lilly is currently conducting the phase 3 SURPASS T1D-1 trial assessing tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Eli Lilly) for people with type 1 diabetes, according to Pettus, who said completion of the trial is scheduled for November.

In addition to moving forward with phase 3 trials and potential submissions to the FDA for approval, Pettus said greater clinician education is needed on incretin-based medications for type 1 diabetes.

“We need to get adoption from clinicians that these drugs are paramount in type 1 diabetes,” Pettus said. “It’s insulin, it’s technology and it’s these metabolic therapies. That is going to take time to get people to reframe what they think about type 1 diabetes.”

Pratley R, et al. Symposium - Dual agonism in type 1 diabetes: Unveiling efficacy and safety of adjunct therapy with CT-868 (GLP-1/GIP RA) in adults with type 1 diabetes – phase 1 and 2 results. Presented at: American Diabetes Association Scientific Sessions; June 5-8, 2026; New Orleans.

Disclosures: Klein reports consulting for Antag Therapeutics, Metsera, Novo Nordisk, Roche and vTv Therapeutics; and receiving research support from Bayer, Boehringer Ingelheim, Carmot, Diasome, Eli Lilly, GentiBio, Novo Nordisk, Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, Roche and vTv Therapeutics. Pettus reports consulting for Kriya Therapeutics and advising for Diasome, Novo Nordisk and Sanofi. The trial was sponsored by Carmot Therapeutics, which was acquired by Roche after the trial began.

https://www.healio.com/news/ophthalmolog.title: Healio AI partners with Holland Foundation for Sight Restoration
https://www.healio.com/news/ophthalmolog.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Healio AI announced an official partnership with The Holland Foundation for Sight Restoration, which is dedicated to helping those with severe ocular surface disease.

“Staying current with the most up to date medical opinions and treatment strategies is at the essence of what it means to be a physician and use best practices to treat patients,” Stephen S. Lane, MD, chair of the board of directors for The Holland Foundation for Sight Restoration (HFSR), said in a press release from The Wyanoke Group. “Today we have wonderful tools at our fingertips to gain these insights with trusted sources of knowledge. I am happy that HFSR has partnered with Healio AI to leverage its trusted corpus of knowledge to eliminate barriers to physicians accessing the most current and comprehensive content whenever and wherever they need it.”

According to the release, Healio AI will now integrate educational content from HFSR, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization, into its core knowledge base, including the fundamentals of the Cincinnati Protocol for stem cell transplantation in patients with severe ocular surface disease. HFSR, which was founded by ophthalmologist Edward J. Holland, MD, will help further Healio AI’s objective of providing trusted, verified AI sources for physicians.

“Bringing a one-of-kind source to a one-of-a-kind platform is a powerful step forward for trusted clinical AI,” Joan-Marie Stiglich, ELS, Chief AI Officer at Healio, said in the release. “In a time when trust matters more than ever, this partnership strengthens our commitment to delivering authoritative, reliable answers backed by the industry’s most respected content.”

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Food preservatives raise risk for CVD, high blood pressure
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Andrew (Drew) Rhoades
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Several frequently used food preservatives may increase the risk for CVD and hypertension, according to findings published in European Heart Journal.

“These new data call for a re-evaluation of the safety of food additive preservatives by health authorities for better consumer protection,” lead study author Anaïs Hasenböhler, a PhD student at Sorbonne Paris North University in France, told Healio. “This may lead to eliminating some of these preservatives from the market or lowering authorized doses.”

Hasenböhler and colleagues previously reported that higher consumption of food preservatives increased the risk for type 2 diabetes from 40% to 49%.

In the current analysis, the researchers assessed the 2009 to 2024 dietary data of 112,395 participants (mean age, 42.8 years; 78.7% women) in the NutriNet-Santé study.

The researchers assessed participants’ diets through 24-hour dietary records. They followed participants for a median 7.9 years.

Nearly all (99.5%) of the cohort consumed at least one preservative within the first 2 years of the study, according to a press release. A total of 58 preservatives had been consumed by at least one participant.

Hasenböhler and colleagues found that higher intake of total non-antioxidant preservatives raised the risk for hypertension by 29% (HR = 1.29; 95% CI, 1.2-1.39) and CVD by 16% (HR = 1.16; 95% CI, 1.04-1.29) vs. lower consumption, whereas greater intake of total antioxidant preservatives was tied to a 22% higher risk for hypertension (HR = 1.22; 95% CI, 1.13-1.31).

Eight of the 17 individual food preservatives consumed by at least 10% of the cohort — including potassium sorbate, ascorbic acid, rosemary extracts, sodium ascorbate, potassium metabisulphite, citric acid, sodium nitrite and sodium erythorbate — were linked to a higher risk for hypertension, the release said, while ascorbic acid was also tied to a higher CVD risk.

Previous research suggests that food preservatives may alter the gut microbiota, the liver or pancreatic functions, which could be contributing to the adverse cardiovascular outcomes, Hasenböhler said.

“Type 2 diabetes is indeed also a risk factor for cardiovascular health. In our study, we found that preservatives may increase the incidence of hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and in turn the incidence of CVD,” she said.

Senior study author Mathilde Touvier, PhD, a research professor at the French National Institute for Health and Medical Research, told Healio that the findings “support the recommendations to favor non- to minimally processed foods and avoid superfluous additives. Patients’ health care professionals and clinicians could play a key role in disseminating these recommendations to the general population.”

“If patients are to purchase vegetables, it is recommended for them to look for fresh, uncooked, unprocessed items, or if they are looking for the fastest to prepare and eat, to favor frozen options, which are preserved through a low temperature, not necessarily through the addition of food additive preservatives,” Touvier said.

The researchers acknowledged that the study could not prove causality, and residual confounding “cannot be entirely ruled out. However, models were adjusted for a wide range of potential confounders and remained robust across multiple sensitivity analyses.”

Hasenböhler told Healio that the researchers “are currently exploring blood biomarkers of inflammation, oxidative stress and metabolic perturbations, as well as gut microbiota composition of NutriNet-Santé participants in association with their exposures to food additives (preservatives and others, plus mixtures) to better understand mechanisms underlying the associations we observed with disease risk.”

Anaïs Hasenböhler and Mathilde Touvier, PhD, can be reached at primarycare@healio.com.

Hasenböhler A, et al. Eur Heart J. 2026;doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehag308.

Disclosures: Hasenböhler and colleagues report no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Will new reforms fix the ‘fundamentally broken’ PBM system?
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Emma Bascom
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

The recent federal reforms to pharmacy benefit managers are a meaningful step in the right direction, but the work is not over yet, according to experts.

In January 2025, the Federal Trade Commission released a report that revealed pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) overcharged for specialty generic medications — in many cases by hundreds and thousands of percent — for billions in profits. And, according to a report on U.S. Pharmacies and Pharmacy Benefit Managers, the three largest PBMs in the United States — Optum Rx (a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group), Caremark Rx (a subsidiary of CVS Health Corporation, which also owns Aetna and CVS Pharmacy) and Express Scripts (a subsidiary of Cigna) — processed 80% of all equivalent prescription claims in 2025.

But on Feb. 3, Congress passed and President Trump signed a spending package that included reforms to the way PBMs operate.

According to reporting from The New York Times, one of the most notable changes will apply to Medicare-covered drugs: in 2028, a percentage of a drug’s sticker price will no longer be paid out to PBMs. Rather, they will receive flat fees, “a move to try to discourage the benefit managers from pushing high-priced drugs when cheaper alternatives are available.”

In the private sector, PBMs will also see new disclosure requirements regarding details about how an employer’s money is used. Additionally, PBMs will be forced to send all rebates to their employers. According to The Times, “the biggest PBMs say they are already doing that nearly all the time, but employers have complained that PBMs sometimes secretly keep a share of the money.”

“While not perfect, it is deeply encouraging to see Congress, the Department of Labor and the FTC finally recognizing what so many of us have warned for years: the PBM marketplace is fundamentally broken,” Madelaine Feldman, MD, FACR, vice president of advocacy and government affairs for the Coalition of State Rheumatology Organizations, told Healio. “For too long, PBMs have operated through anticompetitive, deceptive, opaque and, at times, fraudulent practices that drive up drug costs while harming patients, providers, employers, unions and pharmacists alike.”

Feldman said that PBMs “began as administrators of pharmacy claims,” but “have had a gigantic mission creep over the years.” In 1974, for example, “they gained control over employer-funded prescription plans with the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA),” which allowed large employers to offer prescription benefits. Then, in 1991, PBMs “received ‘safe harbor’ from the anti-kickback statute, allowing manufacturers to kickback rebates to PBMs for formulary placement.” That has allowed PBMs “to create formularies with preference for higher priced drugs,” since the rebates they receive are a percentage of the drug’s sticker price.

“Consequently, competition to get on the formulary has led to higher and higher priced drugs over the years,” Feldman said. “As PBMs instituted utilization management tools, such as prior authorization, step therapy and nonmedical switching, they have usurped the physicians’ place in deciding what medications our patients can take and in what order they can take them. Ultimately, this results in patients taking the medications that are most profitable to the PBM.”

Feldman also said that PBMs have become “the creators of the pharmacy networks that would be covered by the health insurance plan, leading to steering of patients to pharmacies that they or their mother company owned,” which “extended PBM control over not only what drugs patients can take but where they can get them.”

“Clearly, reform is needed to increase transparency and bring more legitimate competition to this opaque, anticompetitive system and vertically integrated system,” Feldman said.

Sumedh Mankar, DO, MPH, FCAPM, a triple board-certified osteopathic physician specializing in family medicine, said that PBMs generate revenue in a few key ways:

Mankar said that “the new provisions aim to decouple PBM compensation in Medicare Part D from the list price of medications and from manufacturer rebate arrangements.”

“In simple terms, PBMs will no longer earn greater compensation simply because a drug has a higher price or larger rebate. PBMs will also be required to pass 100% of manufacturer rebates to the payor, rather than retaining a portion of those rebates,” he said. “In addition, the new rules require greater transparency and reporting from PBMs, which is an important step toward better oversight of the prescription drug supply chain.”

The changes “are intended to reduce some of the misaligned incentives that have historically existed within the PBM business model,” but “it is important to note that the recent reforms primarily apply to Medicare Part D prescription drug plans,” Mankar said.

“While these provisions may influence practices in the commercial insurance market, they do not yet fully extend to Medicaid programs,” he said.

Feldman said the reforms — especially regarding rebates — are “a great step in the right direction. This essentially accomplishes delinking of the price of the drug from the compensation. In fully funded plans, the rebates are passed back to the carrier. This could be just a ‘moving money from the left pocket to the right pocket’ scenario, [but] hopefully, transparency of the amounts will force the carrier to use those rebates to lower premiums.”

However, she noted that “there is some question about the granularity that is needed in these pass throughs and disclosures,” as PBMs “seem to think aggregate disclosures are sufficient. Semiannual reports are required and spread pricing in exchange plans has to be reported along with drug pricing and formulary rationales. PBMs have to make their rebate records available for audit — again, the granularity of the audit records may be in dispute,” Feldman said. “There are penalties, but as we have seen, the penalties are so small compared with the profits PBMs make on violations, in some cases it is just a slap on the wrist.”

Feldman also noted that, under ERISA, PBMs will be designated as covered service providers, “which will help strengthen fiduciary oversight of the compensation, but not necessarily declare the PBMs are fiduciaries of the plan.” However, “there is a bill that would do that. We need the bipartisan PBM Fiduciary Accountability, Integrity, and Reform (FAIR) Act, introduced in Congress in late 2025, which aims to amend ERISA and classify PBMs as fiduciaries, meaning they would have to act in the best interest of the plans and the beneficiaries.”

As far as the direct impact on patients and providers, Feldman said that, for fully funded plans, “it is the hope that premiums might be reduced, but that rarely happens.

“Additionally, it is hoped that transparency of price concessions will lead to lower out-of-pocket costs for patients, but there is no mandate to make co-insurance based on post price concession,” Feldman said. “For providers, it is hoped that taking away the incentive for PBMs to use higher priced medications will make formulary construction less geared toward profit — but, somehow, profits always seem to top priority for PBMs.”

A spokesperson for the AMA told Healio that the organization “considers the PBM reforms signed into law as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, a win and a much-needed step in the right direction toward greater transparency in opaque PBM practices. These reforms represent the most significant federal changes to PBM practices in decades. They are aimed primarily at drug-pricing transparency, PBM compensation structures, and oversight, especially in Part D,” the spokesperson said.

According to the AMA, the changes might “make it easier for patients to understand how their prescription drug coverage works and “push PBMs and insurance plans to explain why certain drugs are covered or not.

“Overall, the goal is to make drug pricing more open and reduce hidden fees that make medications more expensive,” the spokesperson said. “For doctors and other providers, these changes could help ensure that decisions about which drugs are covered are based more on what works best for patients, instead of which drugs give the biggest financial rebates to companies.”

Mankar agreed that the reforms signal progress, even though “they do not constitute a complete overhaul of the PBM marketplace. Over time, these changes may improve transparency and reduce incentives to favor high-list-price, high-rebate drugs when lower-cost alternatives are available. This could eventually lead to a better aligned formulary design and potentially improve affordability for patients.”

However, Mankar said “further reforms are still needed. Future policy efforts may need to address several areas, including extending protections to Medicaid programs, limiting spread pricing practices nationally, addressing the impact of vertical integration and strengthening safeguards to decrease formulary manipulation to ensure that lower-cost, clinically appropriate medications are placed properly.”

Some are trying to take action at the state-level. For example, the Missouri Attorney General recently sued 19 PBM companies and drug manufacturers that operate in Missouri for insulin prices. Additionally, on May 22, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee signed a PBM reform bill into law. CVS filed a lawsuit against the law on May 26.

According to the Tennessee Bar Association, the Tennessee bill will prevent PBMs from having pharmacy licenses in the state and will require divested pharmacy ownership by July 1, 2028. Feldman said it “prohibits the same entity from owning the PBMs and the retail/mail-in pharmacy and steering them to PBM-owned pharmacies or offering incentives to use them.” It additionally would require “a portion of rebates to be passed on to patients and plan sponsors” and would ensure PBMs cannot charge patients or sponsors more for a medication than the PBM initially paid.

“If the divestiture holds up in court for all plans, including the ERISA plans, this will be a huge win affecting employers, patients and providers who have in-house dispensing,” Feldman said. “Removing specialty pharmacy steering to PBM specialty pharmacy drugs will help to reduce the cost of expensive small molecule drugs that go generic, such as the debacle of what happened with the high prices of imatinib (Gleevec, Novartis) when it went generic.”

The AMA spokesperson also noted how the organization’s advocacy made a difference here. For years, it has supported PBM reforms “as the issue also has attracted congressional interest. The AMA publishes annual analyses of market consolidation and has reviewed legislative proposals aimed at increasing transparency and accountability. This remains a priority issue for the AMA House of Delegates, which recognizes the significant influence PBM practices have on pharmaceutical costs and continues to push for meaningful reform. We will continue to monitor areas not addressed in the Continuing Resolution but remain persistent challenges for patients and physicians such as prior authorization and utilization management reforms, as well as concerns related to market concentration and vertical integration.”

Mankar said that PCPs can also “play an important role in advocacy efforts through local, state and national medical organizations to support policies that improve transparency, affordability and patient access within the prescription drug system. Policymakers often value direct input from practicing physicians when evaluating health care policy.”

Ultimately, Mankar said PCPs must “remain attentive to formulary design and to prescribe lower-cost, therapeutically equivalent medications whenever possible. Physicians should also be aware that manufacturer assistance programs, rebates or other affordability programs may be available for certain specialty or high-cost medications and can sometimes help patients access needed therapies.”

Madelaine Feldman, MD, FACR, and the AMA spokesperson can be reached at primarycare@healio.com. Sumedh Mankar, DO, MPH, FCAPM, can be reached on LinkedIn at https://www.linkedin.com/in/sumedh-mankar-do-mph-fcapm-0832388b/.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Adverse pregnancy outcomes linked to poor CV health in offspring
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Adverse pregnancy outcomes, especially hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, were associated with poor cardiovascular health in offspring by early adulthood, researchers reported in JAMA Network Open.

“Most adults in the United States are at elevated risk for heart disease. We are learning that this risk can be passed to future generations, and it’s not related only to genetics,” Nilay S. Shah, MD, MPH, FAHA, FACC, assistant professor of cardiology, preventive medicine and medical social sciences at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, told Healio. “This transmission across generations is potentially preventable, and we investigated how health during pregnancy might influence the health of children decades later as they are young adults.”

Shah and colleagues analyzed data from 1,333 offspring participants from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study and Future of Families – Cardiovascular Health Among Young Adults study (mean age at young adulthood, 22.5 years; 55% women). All participants at age 22 years underwent assessment by the American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 score, had clinical CV risk factors documented and had carotid ultrasonography to determine arterial injury.

Among the cohort, 10% had been exposed to a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, 5% to gestational diabetes and 10% to preterm birth, the researchers wrote.

After adjustment for sociodemographic factors, exposure to a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy was associated with elevated BMI (adjusted beta, 2.8; 95% CI, 1.07-4.53), elevated diastolic BP (adjusted beta, 2.29; 95% CI, 0.17-4.41), elevated HbA1c (adjusted beta, 0.21; 95% CI, 0.02-0.41), elevated carotid intima-media thickness (adjusted beta, 0.02; 95% CI, 0.01-0.03) and lower carotid gray scale median (adjusted beta,3.68; 95% CI,6.3 to 1.05) as a young adult, Shah and colleagues found.

In addition, exposure to gestational diabetes was associated with elevated carotid intima-media thickness (adjusted beta, 0.02; 95% CI, 0-0.04) and lower Life’s Essential 8 BP score (adjusted beta, 6.59; 95% CI,13.95 to 0.16) and exposure to preterm birth was associated with elevated HbA1c (adjusted beta, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.15-0.43), they found.

“Before this study, we knew that mothers’ health during pregnancy influenced their children’s health,” Shah told Healio. “What our study shows is that the child’s exposure to these cardiovascular and metabolic conditions while in utero may influence their heart health decades later when they are young adults. This was most surprising to me — that these very early life exposures while a child is still developing in utero may have long-reaching health effects more than 2 decades later. There is good evidence to suggest that a mother’s health before pregnancy influences their risk of experiencing these adverse pregnancy outcomes. So, we need to do a better job helping people maintain good health as they transition from adolescence into young adulthood and especially as they enter reproductive age.”

The cycle of poor CV health passed through generations can be stopped with early intervention, Shah said.

“The good news is that most heart disease is preventable. If a mother experienced high blood pressure or high blood sugar during pregnancy, or their child was born early (preterm), it does not absolutely mean that the child will have worse health as an adult,” Shah told Healio. “But I would encourage all parents (mothers and fathers alike) to pay attention now to your child’s health behaviors. What children learn in childhood sets the stage for their health across their lives. Heart-healthy behaviors (like getting regular exercise and physical activity, eating a healthful diet, never smoking) are habits that start in childhood. It’s not too early to follow heart healthful behaviors. If anyone is wondering whether their children’s behaviors are healthy, or are considering making a change, they should speak with their child’s pediatrician for advice and guidance — they are an important resource who can help make sure your children develop healthy habits now and as they grow.”

Nilay S. Shah, MD, MPH, FAHA, FACC, assistant professor of cardiology, preventive medicine and medical social sciences, and general and preventive cardiologist in the Bluhm Cardiovascular Institute at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, can be reached at nilay.shah@northwestern.edu.

Lam EL, et al. JAMA Netw Open. 2026;doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.6783.

Disclosures: The authors report no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/gastroentero.title: Hepatic steatosis linked to cardiovascular risk, plaque burden
https://www.healio.com/news/gastroentero.author: Octavia Feliciano
https://www.healio.com/news/gastroentero.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Individuals with hepatic steatosis appeared to have higher amounts of noncalcified coronary plaque and were almost twice as likely to experience major adverse cardiovascular events compared with those without fatty liver disease, data show.

Noncalcified plaque, which is lipid rich and susceptible to rupture that can lead to blood clots, accounted for approximately 11% of this elevated risk. The raised risk suggests that plaque burden is an important contributor, but that additional pathways also are likely involved.

“In hepatic steatosis, the cardiovascular risk is carried not only by how much plaque is present but also by what the plaque is made of,” first author Jan M. Brendel, MD, postdoctoral research fellow at the Cardiovascular Imaging Research Center at Massachusetts General Hospital, told Healio.

Around 30% to 40% of the U.S. population has hepatic steatosis, according to prior research, making it a common issue for Americans. The leading cause of death for individuals with the condition is cardiovascular disease, so the two share a key diagnostic connection.

“A hepatic steatosis diagnosis should trigger cardiovascular risk assessment and coordination with cardiology or primary care, not hepatic follow-up alone,” Brendel said.

Brendel and colleagues investigated the relationship between coronary plaque composition, hepatic steatosis and cardiovascular risk using data from the PROMISE trial, a multicenter study of stable outpatients with chest pain and no prior coronary artery disease.

“The PROMISE trial was well suited to answer this question because its coronary CT arm gave us liver imaging and quantitative, core-lab plaque analysis alongside adjudicated outcomes in the same patients,” Brendel said.

The median follow-up for patients in the trial — conducted between July 2010 and October 2014 — was 25 months.

Brendel and colleagues’ analysis included 3,637 patients (mean age, 60.6 years; 51.4% women) assigned to undergo coronary CT angiography to measure plaque burden and composition.

More than a quarter (25.5%) of these patients had hepatic steatosis.

Hepatic steatosis was linked to greater noncalcified plaque burden (beta = 15%; 95% CI, 4%-27%) and increased risk for major adverse cardiovascular events (adjusted HR = 1.69; 95% CI, 1.12-2.54), independent of other risk factors like obesity and coronary stenosis.

Individuals with hepatic steatosis also had 24% more noncalcified plaque volume than those without the condition.

“Noncalcified plaque explained only about 11% of the excess cardiovascular risk,” Brendel said. “Even after accounting for plaque composition, hepatic steatosis remained independently linked to major adverse cardiovascular events. That indicates plaque is one pathway among several, and that the liver-coronary connection runs deeper than what we can see on the coronary CT angiogram.”

Brendel and colleagues used imaging data and cardiovascular risk factors assessed only at baseline, so they could not investigate changes in liver disease or plaque characteristics over time.

“The most important next step is prospective, longitudinal work using serial coronary CT to test whether treating the metabolic disease — through weight loss, dietary changes, exercise, avoiding alcohol, intensive lipid-lowering, GLP-1 receptor agonists or emerging metabolic agents — actually slows or reverses noncalcified plaque and translates into fewer events,” Brendel said.

He emphasized that noncalcified plaque burden is a modifiable risk factor.

“The logical strategy is to treat the liver and the arteries as one cardiometabolic problem,” Brendel told Healio. “The goal would be to identify high-risk patients earlier — ideally using their existing imaging — and intervene before vulnerable plaque becomes a clinical event.”

Jan M. Brendel, MD, can be reached at gastroenterology@healio.com.

Brendel JM, et al. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2026;doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2026.04.022.

Disclosures: Brendel reports funding from Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft. Please see the study for all other authors’ relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: AI models can identify people at risk for cardiac arrest
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Use of AI-enhanced ECGs and electronic health records enabled researchers to distinguish people at high risk for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, according to data published in JACC: Advances.

“There to date remains no established, validated approach for cardiac arrest screening in the general population,” Neal Chatterjee, MD, MSc, associate professor of medicine at the University of Washington School of Medicine, told Healio. “Our work highlights a couple of things. No. 1, the factors that are driving cardiac arrest risk, to some extent, are cardiovascular, but there’s a large amount of that risk that is noncardiovascular. No. 2, we can more narrowly tailor our risk prediction for this particular outcome.”

Chatterjee and colleagues conducted a case-control study to derive and validate the model with AI-enhanced ECGs and EHR data and to evaluate the 2-year incidence of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in patients who underwent ECGs at UW Medicine while accounting for the competing risk of death from other causes.

“Previous studies in cardiac arrest have looked generally at the ability of models differentiate between an individual with cardiac arrest compared to an individual without,” Chatterjee told Healio. “What was missing, however, was a direct evaluation of how these models would perform in a real-world setting. In this paper, we specifically looked at individuals coming into the UW health system over a 1-year period. We then applied our models to these individuals and followed them for 2 years into the future. Over that 2-year time frame, we were able to flag a high-risk group of patients with a risk of about 1% per year. That’s a huge improvement over the baseline risk for individuals in the general population (one in 1,000 per year).”

The model with AI-enhanced ECGs and EHR data had higher discrimination for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.83; area under the precision recall curve, 0.44) compared with ECGs alone or EHR data alone (Bonferroni-adjusted P for all < .05), the researchers wrote.

In the real-world cohort of 39,911 patients who had an ECG in 2021, those identified by the model as high risk for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest had a 2-year cumulative incidence of cardiac arrest of 2.4% (95% CI, 2%-2.8%), compared with 0.5% (95% CI, 0.3%-0.8%) for those identified as being at low risk, according to the researchers.

“This model, for the first time, demonstrates that we can enrich the risk of cardiac arrest about 20-fold,” Chatterjee told Healio. “Practically speaking, we are able to identify a high-risk group in the general population where we transform risk from about one in 1,000 per year to about one to two in 100 per year. For a patient, understanding and digesting a 1% to 2% risk feels very different than a one in 1,000 risk.”

Before the model can become widely adopted, it will have to be validated in other settings, Chatterjee said.

Also important, he said, is “not using this technology to create the ‘worried well.’ In other words, we want to avoid undue anxiety, psychological stress and additional testing in otherwise healthy individuals. To resolve this, we need to now understand what subsequent testing these models should justify. Practically speaking, we see this work as a key and necessary first step in this bigger story. We are actively pursuing external funding opportunities to understand what a systematic screening protocol would look like for ‘high-risk’ individuals. Testing could include genetic evaluation, more advanced cardiac imaging and continuous rhythm monitoring. After that layer of testing, if there were abnormalities, future testing could include even more complex approaches such as virtual or digital twin technology to evaluate arrhythmia risk. Beyond the general population, we are also now evaluating [whether] there are certain populations that might benefit most from this sort of screening. Possible groups include those with a family history of heart disease or cardiac arrest, athletes (who represent a high profile subgroup of individuals at risk) and certain clinical contexts (eg, hospitalization for heart condition or syncope).”

If someone is identified as high risk by the model, “the practical intervention for that patient may be something like a defibrillator,” Chatterjee told Healio. “At the moment, we generally reserve something like a defibrillator for very high-risk patients who have significant abnormalities of heart function. But those types of individuals only account for a small slice of the pie in terms of the global burden of cardiac arrest.”

Neal Chatterjee, MD, MSc, associate professor of medicine and John and Cookie Laughlin Endowed Professor in Cardiology at the University of Washington School of Medicine and deputy editor of NEJM Evidence, can be reached at nchatter@uw.edu or on X @nchatterjeemd.

Sharma S, et al. JACC Adv. 2026;doi:10.1016/j.jacadv.2026.102787.

Disclosures: Chatterjee reports no relevant financial disclosures. Please see the study for all other authors’ relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.title: Women more likely to misrepresent Match preferences vs. men
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.author: Lucas Laboy
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Gendered differences may impact how medical students rank their preferred schools when matching for residency, according to study data published in Organization Science.

Across two studies, the data show that men and women navigate the Main Residency Match differently and highlight the need for improved education on the process, according to Samuel E. Skowronek, PhD, assistant professor of management at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business, and Joyce C. He, PhD, assistant professor of management and organizations at UCLA Anderson School of Management.

“The National Resident Matching Program (NRMP) uses a version of the deferred acceptance algorithm, which incentivizes all students to submit an honest rank ordering of their preferred residencies,” Skowronek told Healio. “Our paper explores why this gender effect might exist and what schools might be able to do about it.”

In the first study, the researchers analyzed a simulation of the Main Residency Match with 1,714 graduating medical students (mean age, 27.2 years; 48% women) across 25 U.S. medical schools who had just completed their real Match application in 2017. Each student ranked five fictitious residency programs, with School A offering the highest incentive of $50 and School E offering the lowest of $7.50. Participants would receive $5 if they did not match to any program.

“Because of the incentives of the algorithm, all students should rank A, B, C,D and E in order of financial value, assuming that all students prefer more money to less money, which is an assumption we felt comfortable with,” Skowronek said.

Results showed that women were less likely to submit an optimal rank-ordered list in the Match simulation than men (72% vs. 81%).

Women also reported a significantly lower understanding of how the NRMP worked vs. men.

Men were more likely to independently learn more about the Match algorithm through online research and videos vs. women. In particular, men were more likely to obtain advice from the NRMP website vs. women (45% vs. 35%).

“From these findings, we decided to take a deeper dive into why women were more likely to submit a suboptimal rank-ordered list,” he said.

In the second study, the researchers conducted semistructured interviews with 66 graduating medical students (mean age, 27.3 years; 66% women; 61% Asian) immediately after they had submitted their rank-ordered list to the NRMP to understand how they navigated the Match process in 2023.

From the interviews, several themes emerged. All students said they learned about the Match process through mandatory Zoom webinars and working with assigned faculty members. However, students also reported that “little emphasis” was given to how the algorithm worked and faculty did not inform students to independently research the Match process, the researchers wrote.

Notably, 15 women explicitly said they did not conduct any additional research on the Match process, compared with one man. These differences in advice-seeking may reflect “socialized gender roles,” according to Skowronek.

“When we asked them, most women didn’t feel as though that advice was lacking,” he said, “They just chose not to reinforce or clarify how to navigate the algorithm with additional resources.”

In addition, Skowronek said these differences could reflect a communication issue.

“The advice appears to be so simple, asking students to ‘rank your schools in the way you prefer,’” he said. “Teachers go even further and tell students to just ‘follow your heart’ or ‘trust your gut,’ but this advice is clearly not as simple as it appears.”

Further research is needed to develop the “optimal way to describe the Match algorithm,” for men and women, according to Skowronek.

“The goal isn't simply for applicants to match somewhere; it's for them to maximize their chances of matching to the residency programs they most prefer,” Skowronek said. “Our data suggest that men are more likely than women to use the strategy that best achieves that outcome. As a result, women may be less likely to obtain their preferred placements, even when they successfully match. This disparity is not a feature of the algorithm and may be addressed through improvements in the algorithmic training provided to medical students.”

To do this, educators should focus on describing how the algorithm works and encourage independent research from trusted sources beyond a single informational session, Skowronek and He wrote.

In addition, simulated processes could be beneficial, Skowronek said.

“It seems like being on a Zoom webinar isn’t the right way to teach them about this important feature of the algorithm,” Skowronek said. “My read is that it might be more helpful to place students in the kind of simulation that we created to have them learn how the algorithm works — that could go a long way in teaching medical students how to use it effectively.”

Samuel E. Skowronek, PhD, can be reached at ses239@georgetown.edu.

Skowronek SE, et al. Organization Science. 2026;doi:10.1287/orsc.2024.19652.

Disclosures: The authors report no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: CMS implements work requirements for Medicaid
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Emma Bascom
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CMS has issued an interim final rule that implements new work requirements for adults on Medicaid.

The new statutory requirement will apply to adults who are aged 19 to 64, not pregnant and “enrolled in the Medicaid adult group or in certain section 1115 demonstrations that provide minimum essential coverage to adult beneficiaries,” according to a CMS fact sheet. As of now, 43 states and Washington D.C. offer coverage to these populations and must implement the new requirement.

Those who are affected will now be required to engage in qualifying activities — employment, community service or some work programs — for 80 hours per month, make at least $580 monthly (the minimum wage multiplied by 80 hours), “or be enrolled in educational program for at least half time,” according to CMS. Plus, eligible new applications would need to meet the requirements for a minimum of 1 month before the month they apply, and current beneficiaries must meet the requirement for at least 1 month between renewal.

There are some exceptions, like for those who are medically frail or disabled; caretakers or parents of people with disabilities or children aged 14 years or younger; former foster care youth; inmates of a public institution; participants in a rehabilitation program for drug or alcohol treatment; members of a household receiving Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits and not exempt from SNAP’s work requirements; and for American Indians/Alaska Natives.

“This rule helps Americans build skills and independence through work, education, job training or community service, creating new opportunities for themselves and their families,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, MD, said in a related press release.

States are required to implement the new rules by Jan. 1, 2027. But, according to the release, the rule “is being issued with comment period” as “this approach helps to ensure timely implementation while allowing CMS to continue to collect and consider public feedback.”

In the release, CMS cited a study from the HHS Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation that indicated “the new requirements could reduce poverty by as much as 2.9 million people depending on a variety of conditions such as employment availability.”

However, as Healio previously reported, a recent study revealed that about half of adult beneficiaries — translating to 8.3 million people — could lose their coverage, and many will likely find themselves in a catch-22 by being too impaired to meet the 80-hour monthly work requirement but not enough to qualify for disability.

Darshali A. Vyas, MD, a pulmonary and critical care fellow at Massachusetts General Hospital and the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, told Healio that her top concern “is that this rule locks states into one uniform, narrow and federally defined framework for medical frailty.”

According to the AMA, CMS broadly defines medical frailty as:

“CMS explicitly says states will not have latitude to add additional frailty categories because the agency believes the five outlined categories are sufficient,” Vyas said. “Restricting frailty definitions to just five criteria is a big policy choice. Our research suggests the opposite risk: many Medicaid beneficiaries do not fit neatly into clean administrative boxes.”

In Vyas’s study, “half of working-age Medicaid beneficiaries would be at risk of disenrollment,” and “those at risk had worse physical health, worse mental health and substantially more functional impairment than those meeting work requirements.”

Vyas said the main risk with the rule “is that people who are medically vulnerable but not formally disabled will lose coverage because they are not identified as exempt. The practical question still remains over whether states will actually identify those people. A low-income patient with COPD, heart failure, cognitive impairment, cancer, chronic pain, severe mental illness or functional limitation may not know they qualify as medically frail. They may not have the paperwork. Their clinician may not have documented the limitation in the right way. And if they miss a notice or fail to report correctly, they will still lose coverage despite being exactly the kind of person the exemption is supposed to protect.”

Vyas added that, “ultimately, the rule will either succeed or fail based on implementation. The stakes are especially high for people in the in-between: not ‘disabled enough’ to be obvious to the system, but too medically or functionally limited to reliably meet an 80-hour monthly requirement and navigate a complex reporting process. The take-home message is that exemptions on paper are not the same as protections in actual practice.”

According to a press release from the American Association of People with Disabilities (AAPD), “the research could not be clearer: work requirements do not increase workforce participation or help people get jobs; work requirements get people kicked off of Medicaid. For the millions of Americans with disabilities who depend on Medicaid not just for doctor visits but for the personal care, medications, employment supports, and services that keep them alive and living in their communities, a loss of coverage is not a mere inconvenience; it can be a death sentence.”

The AAPD also noted that the state of Arkansas implemented work requirements from 2018 to 2020, and 18,000 people were disenrolled not “because they were no longer eligible, but rather, because they could not navigate the administrative and bureaucratic barriers of work requirements.”

The AAPD added that “despite the promises made by Congress and exemptions listed in the rule, people with disabilities will not be protected. They will lose their lifeline not because they are ineligible, but because the administrative obstacles created by this guidance are too great to overcome.”

In a statement, ACP President Jan K. Carney, MD, MPH, MACP, said the organization “is strongly opposed” to the work requirements.

“Most adults covered by Medicaid are already working, caregiving or would not be subject to this policy due to illness or disability; research shows us that instituting work requirements will not meaningfully increase employment,” Carney said. “Community engagement requirements create a tangle of red tape that diverts resources away from patient care and worsens the administrative burden on physicians. The Medicaid program is designed to ensure that those most vulnerable among us are able to access needed medical care. Instituting work requirements for the program could lead to millions of individuals losing health care coverage, putting at risk their health, financial security and lives.”

Arthur L. Caplan, PhD, a professor and founding head of the division of medical ethics at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, told Healio that the “obsession with work requirements is just misguided. It’s not that people can’t expect you to work if you can — that’s a fine expectation — but you’ve got to be able to get people jobs that have benefits. A lot of people are working, and they don’t get any benefits from the job.”

“What they should be concentrating on is providing jobs with benefits, not kicking people off because they don’t work,” he said. “I see no evidence that Medicaid is full of able-bodied people hanging out on street corners who just don’t feel like working. I don’t see any evidence of that.”

Vyas also noted the important role of clinicians and health systems in protecting patients.

“If we do not measure and document functional status well, medically vulnerable people will fall through the cracks,” she said. “These updates mean that providers caring for low-income patients should be screening for and documenting functional limitations much more explicitly: difficulty walking, standing, lifting, bathing, dressing, doing errands, managing medications, concentrating, attending appointments or complying with complex paperwork.”

That documentation could become critically important for their recognition as medically frail, Vyas said.

“A diagnosis alone may not be enough. The rule repeatedly focuses on whether the condition significantly impairs the person’s ability to comply with community engagement requirements,” she said. “So, the relevant question is no longer just ‘What disease does this patient have?’ but also ‘How does this disease affect their ability to function, work, report, travel, complete forms and maintain coverage?’ For low-income patients with chronic disease, that distinction could determine whether they keep Medicaid.”

Arthur L. Caplan, PhD, and Darshali A. Vyas, MD, can be reached at primarycare@healio.com.

Disclosures: Caplan and Vyas report no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Bempedoic acid may prevent dangerous blood clots
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Bempedoic acid may prevent dangerous blood clots from forming in addition to reducing risk for major cardiovascular events vs. placebo in statin-intolerant people with prior CVD or at high risk for it, researchers reported.

Bempedoic acid (Nexletol, Esperion Therapeutics) significantly reduced risk for venous thromboembolism, including both deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, compared with placebo, according to a post hoc analysis of the randomized, placebo-controlled CLEAR Outcomes trial published in JAMA Cardiology.

“We know that patients that take statins, particularly rosuvastatin, have a lower risk for VTE. We wanted to assess if bempedoic acid had that same impact,” Luke J. Laffin, MD, associate professor of medicine at Cleveland Clinic, told Healio. “Although it’s a post hoc analysis, the data clearly suggest that similar to statins, bempedoic acid not only protects against atherosclerotic CVD but also deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary emboli.”

As Healio previously reported, in the main results of CLEAR Outcomes, bempedoic acid reduced risk for major CV events by 13% vs. placebo in adults with prior CVD or deemed high risk who were statin intolerant, in addition to lowering risk for MI by 23%.

For the present analysis, researchers evaluated the impact of bempedoic acid on risk for VTE. Other outcomes of interest included DVT and pulmonary embolism.

At baseline, in the overall cohort of 13,970 participants (mean age, 66 years; 48% women), approximately 2% had a history of VTE and 8.7% were taking systemic anticoagulation.

Over a median follow-up of more than 40 months, participants assigned bempedoic acid experienced lower risk for VTE compared with placebo (HR = 0.58; 95% CI, 0.39-0.86; P = .006), according to the study.

The bempedoic acid group had lower risk for DVT (HR = 0.56; 95% CI, 0.31-0.996; P = .045) and pulmonary embolism (HR = 0.61; 95% CI, 0.37-0.996; P = .046) compared with the placebo group, Laffin and colleagues reported.

Numerically more adverse events were observed among patients assigned to bempedoic acid compared with those assigned to placebo, including gout, hyperuricemia, hepatic enzyme elevation, kidney impairment and cholelithiasis; however, formal hypothesis testing was not performed, and P values were not calculated, according to the study.

“We don’t necessarily know why statins and bempedoic acid decrease the risk of venous thromboembolism, but we cannot overlook the anti-inflammatory effects that each have,” Laffin told Healio. “It’s another piece of information that can help guide clinicians’ decisions. Bempedoic acid is now highlighted in the new lipid guidelines as a good choice in patients with statin intolerance to reduce ASCVD risk. This gives us another good reason to prescribe.”

Luke J. Laffin, MD, associate professor of medicine and codirector of the Center for Blood Pressure Disorders at Cleveland Clinic, can be reached at cardiology@healio.com.

Spiazzi BF, et al. JAMA Cardiol. 2026;doi:10.1001/jamacardio.2026.1208.

Disclosures: Laffin reports having contracts with Arrowhead, Eli Lilly and Madrigal through C5Research; receiving personal fees from AstraZeneca; consulting or serving on steering committees for CRISPR Therapeutics, Eli Lilly, Medtronic, Mineralys, Novartis, Novo Nordisk, Recor, Ripple Medical and Stability Health; receiving research funding from AstraZeneca, Arrowhead, Kardigan and Retension; and receiving royalties from Belvoir Media Group and Elsevier. The study was funded by Esperion Therapeutics and coordinated by C5Research.

https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.title: Wegovy confers weight loss, heart-related benefits in menopause
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.author: Michael Monostra
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Once-weekly injectable semaglutide is tied to weight loss and cardiovascular benefits for women regardless of menopause status, according to data from two post hoc analyses presented at the European Congress on Obesity.

“Menopause is more than hot flushes; it’s a cardiometabolic transition,” Emilia Huvinen, MD, PhD, associate professor and specialist in obstetrics and gynecology at University of Helsinki, told Healio. “Semaglutide offers a good option for helping with weight management and improving quality of life in menopausal women. It is also beneficial for CV health among women with preexisting cardiovascular diseases.”

In the first post hoc analysis, Huvinen and colleagues assessed data from women aged 45 years and older who participated in the SELECT trial, where participants were randomly assigned to once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg (Wegovy, Novo Nordisk) or placebo. As Healio previously reported, adults receiving semaglutide in SELECT had a 20% lower risk for major adverse CV outcomes over nearly 40 months of follow-up compared with placebo. Menopause status was self-reported.

The trial included 611 perimenopausal women and 4,251 postmenopausal women. The reduced risk for major adverse CV events observed with semaglutide was similar in perimenopausal women and postmenopausal women. There was no interaction between menopausal status and treatment effect.

In an exploratory analysis of the SELECT trial, researchers examined data among 3,010 men younger than 55 years and 9,722 men aged 55 years and older. Similar to what was observed among women, the risk reduction for major adverse CV events with semaglutide was not different for younger men compared with older men.

In the STEP UP trial, adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes were randomly assigned to once-weekly semaglutide 7.2 mg, semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo for 72 weeks. As Healio previously reported, adults receiving semaglutide 7.2 mg had an 18.7% weight loss at 72 weeks compared with a 15.6% weight loss with the 2.4 mg dose and a 3.9% weight reduction with placebo.

There were 753 women included in the post hoc analysis, of whom 295 were premenopausal, 238 perimenopausal and 220 postmenopausal. Of the participants, 28.5% in the premenopause group, 13.4% of perimenopausal women and 5.9% in postmenopause used hormone therapy at baseline or during the study.

Among those receiving semaglutide 7.2 mg, weight loss at 72 weeks was 22.6% for premenopausal women, 19.7% for perimenopausal women and 19.8% for postmenopausal women. The percentage of waist circumference decrease from baseline to 72 weeks was 17.5% for premenopausal women, 15.6% for perimenopausal women and 15.3% in the postmenopausal group.

The proportion of women who reached 10%, 15%, 20% or 25% or greater weight loss with semaglutide 7.2 mg was greatest in the premenopausal group. Nearly half of participants across all three groups reduced their BMI to normal or overweight range at 72 weeks.

Huvinen said the findings from both post hoc analyses were “comforting” because they revealed how semaglutide can provide benefits for women across the reproductive lifespan.

“These were post hoc analyses, so we need prospective trials with detailed classification of menopausal status, symptoms and other confounding factors to fully understand this important metabolic transition and to more profoundly be able to help our patients,” Huvinen said. “It would also be beneficial to understand, can effective obesity treatment improve severe menopausal symptoms, especially if started in the premenopausal stage?”

Emilia Huvinen, MD, PhD, an associate professor and specialist in obstetrics and gynecology at University of Helsinki and Helsinki University Hospital, can be reached at emilia.huvinen@helsinki.fi; LinkedIn @emiliahuvinen; X @dremiliahuvinen.

Huvinen E, et al. AS02.04. Presented at: European Congress on Obesity; May 12-15, 2026; Istanbul.

Disclosures: Huvinen reports consulting and receiving honoraria for scientific talks from Boehringer Ingelheim, Eli Lilly, Exeltis, Geden Richter, Merck, Navamedic, Novartis, Novo Nordisk, Orion Pharma and Vivus.

https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.title: Survey: What health care professionals want from AI tools
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.author: Lucas Laboy
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Health care professionals want AI tools that are clinically accurate, offer privacy protections and can be integrated into existing workflows, according to data from a Healio survey.

In March, Healio fielded a 27-item survey to understand how health care professionals are using AI in practice and their sentiments toward AI tools. Among 618 eligible respondents (49.5% men), 52.3% were physicians and 48.4% had more than 21 years of experience. Respondents’ primary affiliations were with private practices (45.1%), academic medical centers (21.4%) and community hospitals (19.9%), among other practice settings.

Results showed that more than 70% of health care professionals use AI tools in their practices at least occasionally, and 69.3% have used AI during patient interactions.

Respondents use AI tools for documentation and note generation (44.5%), synthesizing research (42.9%) and clinical decision support (36.9%). More specifically, 48.8% of respondents who reported using AI regularly or occasionally use it for clinical decision support.

Among respondents who reported using AI tools professionally, 73.3% viewed AI’s impact on their workflow as positive and 2.5% viewed AI’s impact as negative.

A greater proportion of health care professionals reported moderate to great trust in AI for general use vs. professional use (72.5% vs. 65.2%). About one-third of respondents reported low or very low trust in AI, but 44% of “low trust” respondents reported using AI at least occasionally in practice.

Jonathan B. Singer, PhD, LCSW, a Healio AI Advisory Board Member, told Healio that health care professionals may still use AI despite their distrust for a variety of reasons. Some professionals may use AI tools to gauge their trustworthiness for certain tasks or if their patients are using the tools and have questions about AI, he said. Others may have “little or no choice” to opt out based on how AI is integrated into their workflows, Singer said.

“A provider who is skeptical of AI tools might use them with the intention of deciding ‘if’ and ‘when’ the tool can be trusted,” Singer said. “This type of skepticism or distrust is ethical and protective for the patient and the provider.”

Other health care professionals may distinguish private and professional use, according to Singer.

“For example, I trust GenAI to explain why my basement has 17 different types of piping and conduit in the ceiling, but I don’t trust the same GenAI tool to maintain data privacy,” he said.

Nearly 70% of respondents receive organizational support to use AI in clinical care. However, 16% of respondents reported having clear and comprehensive AI policies in place. More than one-quarter said their organization had no formal AI policy and 11.3% of respondents reported receiving institutional training.

Furthermore, 17% of respondents reported being involved in AI discussions and governance within their organization.

Health care professionals cited clinical diagnosis support (40.3%), research and guideline synthesis (20.7%) and medication safety support (17.3%) as the most important uses they wanted for AI in clinical care.

The top influences cited by respondents for selecting an AI tool to use included clinical accuracy (49.7%), data privacy and protections (46.9%) and integration into existing workflows (45.6%).

In addition, respondents rated having information from large and reputable databases, accurate and current information and health care professional involvement in development as the most influential factors for trust in the AI tools they choose to use. More than 90% of respondents reported clinicians should be primarily involved in designing and selecting AI tools.

“More physicians are leaning into AI to help in our professional lives, but at the same time many of us don’t trust it and worry about the accuracy, legal ramifications and the ‘deskilling’ that could happen,” Hansa Bhargava, MD, Healio’s chief clinical strategy and innovation officer, told Healio. “I hope that clinicians are able to take the time and learn about how an LLM [large language model] works, its data sources, how up-to-date the information is and whether doctors have advised on the development of the tool.”

Overall, the findings highlight the importance of trust, accuracy and clinician involvement in AI tool development as health care professionals navigate the evolving field of AI, according to Singer.

“We want providers who are curious about technology, but who approach tools with skepticism,” Singer said. “Allowing providers the option to audit AI responses will help them to decide whether or not to trust the output based on the professional language, verifiable peer-reviewed references, etc.”

Hansa Bhargava, MD, can be reached at primarycare@healio.com.

Jonathan B. Singer, PhD, LCSW, is a professor in the School of Social Work at Loyola University Chicago, founder and host of “The Social Work Podcast” and a member of the Healio Psychiatry Peer Perspective Board and Healio AI Advisory Board. He can be reached at jsinger1@luc.edu.

HCP AI usage survey. Fielded March 16-April 1, 2026.

Disclosures: Bhargava reports being part of the development of Healio AI. Singer reports no relevant financial disclosures.
